lesson.title: Das Geheimnis der Bibliothek
lesson.subtitle: A book falls in a library-bar, and a letter hides a treasure

hook.title: Before You Read
hook.content: This is a capstone reading: a mystery scene with a hook and an open ending. Read for four things — the place, the noise, the object, and what the letter says. The grammar is familiar: Perfekt, dative, and a subclause or two. The new words are glossed so the mystery stays in front of you.

footnotes.title: Geräusch & Boden
footnotes.content: das Geräusch = noise; der Boden = floor. Ein Buch ist auf den Boden gefallen = a book has fallen to the floor.

footnotes.title: Schatz & Geheimnis
footnotes.content: der Schatz = treasure; das Geheimnis = secret. The story is built on the second, and the letter promises the first.

footnotes.title: aufheben
footnotes.content: aufheben = to pick up. Sie hebt es auf = she picks it up. The separable prefix auf flies to the end.

footnotes.title: Trotzdem
footnotes.content: trotzdem = nevertheless / all the same. It signals the story's feeling: they do not find the treasure, but they are happy.

footnotes.title: Bar, Geschichte, Abenteuer
footnotes.content: die Bar = bar; die Geschichte = story; das Abenteuer = adventure. The house is a library with a bar, and the letter tells a story.

pattern.title: Die Geschichte
pattern.content:
Paul arbeitet in einem besonderen Haus. In diesem Haus gibt es viele Bücher, aber auch eine Bar. Die Leute kommen, lesen und trinken.

Heute hilft ihm seine Freundin Paula. Eine Gruppe feiert Geburtstag. Es wird ein langer Abend.

Plötzlich hören Paul und Paula ein lautes Geräusch: BUMM! Ein Buch ist auf den Boden gefallen. Paula geht nach hinten. Dort steht ein altes Buch. Sie hebt es auf und findet einen kleinen Brief.

Paul und Paula lesen den Brief zusammen. Der Brief erzählt eine alte Geschichte: In dem Haus gibt es einen Schatz!

Sie suchen den ganzen Abend, aber sie finden den Schatz nicht. Sie müssen ein anderes Mal weitersuchen. Trotzdem sind sie glücklich. Ein Haus voller Bücher ist immer ein Abenteuer.

exercises.prompt: Reading check — match each story sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Paul works in a special house.
matching_pairs.german: Paul arbeitet in einem besonderen Haus.

matching_pairs.english: In this house there are many books and a bar.
matching_pairs.german: In diesem Haus gibt es viele Bücher und eine Bar.

matching_pairs.english: Suddenly they hear a loud noise.
matching_pairs.german: Plötzlich hören sie ein lautes Geräusch.

matching_pairs.english: A book has fallen to the floor.
matching_pairs.german: Ein Buch ist auf den Boden gefallen.

matching_pairs.english: They search all evening but do not find the treasure.
matching_pairs.german: Sie suchen den ganzen Abend, aber sie finden den Schatz nicht.

exercises.target_answer: Paul arbeitet in einem besonderen Haus., In diesem Haus gibt es viele Bücher und eine Bar., Plötzlich hören sie ein lautes Geräusch., Ein Buch ist auf den Boden gefallen., Paula findet einen kleinen Brief., Sie suchen den ganzen Abend, aber sie finden den Schatz nicht.
exercises.meaning: the mystery beats: the place, the noise, the fallen book, the letter, the search
exercises.explanation: Every beat adds one piece of the mystery. The ending deliberately leaves the search unfinished.

exercises.prompt: What kind of place is Paul's workplace?
exercises.meaning: Paul works in a book-filled house that also has a bar.
exercises.explanation: The text never says Bibliothek, but it describes one: viele Bücher, eine Bar, die Leute kommen, lesen und trinken.

options: A book falls to the floor.
exercises.target_answer: A book falls to the floor.
exercises.meaning: The noise is a book falling to the floor.
exercises.explanation: The colon after Geräusch explains it: Ein Buch ist auf den Boden gefallen. The mystery starts with a small accident.

exercises.prompt: What does the letter talk about?
exercises.meaning: The letter tells an old story about a treasure in the house.
exercises.explanation: Der Brief erzählt eine alte Geschichte: In dem Haus gibt es einen Schatz! The treasure is the letter's promise, not something they find that night.

exercises.prompt: Render the thought in German: 'They find an old book with a letter.'
exercises.idea: They find an old book with a letter.
cues: Start with Sie finden — present tense is enough.
ein altes Buch: the adjective takes -es after ein (neuter).
mit einem Brief is the dative accompaniment.
exercises.target_answer: Sie finden ein altes Buch mit einem Brief
exercises.meaning: They find an old book with a letter.
exercises.explanation: ein altes Buch (neuter nominative/accusative after ein) and mit einem Brief (dative) show two case jobs in one short sentence.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — say in German: 'They do not find the book.'
twist.explanation: nicht comes after the accusative object: Sie finden das Buch nicht. The letter (Brief) is in the story, but this sentence is about the book.

summary.outcome: Read a mystery passage, identify its turning points, and distinguish what happens from what is promised.

use_example.german: Sie finden den Schatz nicht, aber sie sind trotzdem glücklich.
use_example.english: They do not find the treasure, but they are happy all the same.

summary.takeaway: A mystery can end without a solution. The story's job is to make the search interesting, not to hand you the treasure.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: a Monday morning, a thermometer, and a plan that fails.

brief.context_phrase: Ich schreibe einen Brief an Oma.
brief.context_translation: I am writing a letter to Grandma.
brief.etymology_derivation: From Latin breve, the neuter of brevis, short, first for a short papal document; the page lists English brief as a cognate borrowed from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

suchen.context_translation: I am looking for my glasses.
suchen.etymology_derivation: k → ch. Direct transitive object without prepositions.

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

boden.context_translation: The floor is made of wood.
boden.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *budm-, variant of *butmaz — explicitly cognate with English bottom. [wiktionary]

geschenk.etymology_derivation: ge- + schenken (pour, serve); no English cognate — memorize this one (das Gift is the trap word). [wiktionary]

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

freund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, 'the loving one' — the exact twin of English friend. [wiktionary]

gruppe.context_phrase: Unsere Gruppe trifft sich um acht.
gruppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, ultimately from Germanic *kruppaz, lump — the same Romance round-trip word as English group. [wiktionary]

geburtstag.etymology_derivation: Geburt + Tag, exactly English birthday; the Tag/day pair shows the d to t stop shift, and Geburt comes from the gebären family. [wiktionary]

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

stuhl.context_translation: The chair stands at the table.
stuhl.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stōl — cognate with English stool; the meaning narrowed from stool to chair. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

zimmer.context_phrase: Mein Zimmer ist groß und hell.
zimmer.context_translation: My room is big and bright.
zimmer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *timrą — cognate with English timber: English keeps t, German shifted it to z. [wiktionary]

geld.context_translation: I have no money with me.
geld.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *geldą 'reward, payment' — kin to English geld and yield, NOT to gold. [wiktionary]

wort.etymology_derivation: Final d → t. Plural: Wörter / Worte.

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
